To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cadmium exposure to pregnant rats results in decreased absorption of essential metals in duodenal mucosae, and in consequence, in diminished concentration of these metals in maternal serum and in fetal liver.

cadmium given to pregnant rats per os in low dose (6. 25 microg Cd/ml of drinking water) for the first 20 days of gestations, causes a decrease in the concentration of Cu, Zn, and Fe in the duodenums, and in serum, and in activity of ceruloplasmine.
the cadmium-induced decrease in fetal liver Cu and Fe content may be due to the diminished absorption of these metals in the maternal intestines exposed to this toxic metal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of MT and Cp in the mechanism of cadmium toxicity in pregnant dams and their fetuses.
the mechanism of the influence of cadmium on the absorption of Cu and Fe and the role of MT and Cp in the mechanism of this process.
the influence of Cd on the metabolism of Cu and Fe during pregnancy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cadmium exposure of dams to low doses of cadmium in drinking waters during pregnancy may be a risk for the fetal liver.

the Cd-induced changes in the fetal liver Cu and Fe contents are related to the Cd-induced changes of the dam's duodenal mucosal Cu and Fe contents, which is a consequence of the Cd-induced decrease of the dam's blood Cp activity and serum Cu and Fe concentrations.

the mechanism of the deficit of Zn, Cu and Fe content in fetuses after maternal exposure to Cd is based on the reduction of the absorption of these metals in the intestines of dam and on the diminution in metal contents in blood serum and their decreasing availability in fetal liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cadmium exposure to the dam can influence the availability of Zn, Cu and Fe for fetal development.

cadmium exposure in drinking water of dams leads to a reduction of Zn, Cu and Fe concentrations, as well as Cp activity, in serum of blood of dams, which is related to the diminution of availability of these metals in fetuses.
cadmium is a toxic metal, which can disturb the absorption of essential metals, especially in the case of pregnant dams, which can be reflected in the fetus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cadmium exposure to pregnant rats causes a significant decrease in Cu and Cp activity in maternal serum, which leads to a decrease in fetal liver Cu content.

the mechanism of the Cu and Fe deficit in the fetal livers is based on the reduction of absorption of these elements by dam intestines, the reduction of metal content in blood serum, and the reduction of availability in fetuses.
the maternal exposure to cadmium in drinking water may cause a decrease in the availability of essential metals in the fetal liver.
